quantity.quote: This 'Phase I' detector which comprised of 1600 proportional counters having a total weight of 140 tons of iron, was installed deep underground at the depth of 7000 hg/cm2 and started making observations on possible proton decay phenomenon at the end of 1980.
This detector became operational in 1985. The Phase II detector comprised of about 4000 proportional counters and total weight of 260 tons.

name: Kolar Gold Fields experiments
notes: Scope: the series of Tata Institute (TIFR) / Osaka City University underground experiments at Kolar Gold Fields from 1960 to 1993: cosmic-ray muon depth-intensity measurements, the atmospheric-neutrino telescopes of 1965 and the Phase I and II proton-decay detectors. The Indian Neutrino Observatory (INO), a later proposal, is a separate project.

The collaboration's claim of proton decay at about 1e31 years conflicts with the limits of about 1e33 years from other experiments, as the collaboration's own paper acknowledges: "Contrary to this conclusion, as shown in our earlier reports (Ref. 9), our result is that protons are decaying with lifetime of about 10 31 years."
No official website exists (the experiments ended in 1993); none is recorded.

physics_goals.quote: Deep underground in Kolar Gold Fields, in southern India, an experiment to detect proton decay had been carried out since the end of 1980.
physics_goals.value: Search for proton decay deep underground

physics_goals.quote: A series of seven neutrino telescopes were quickly set up at a depth of 2300 m and in early 1965 they recorded the first atmospheric-neutrino event
physics_goals.value: Detect neutrinos produced by cosmic rays in the atmosphere deep underground

summary.plain: Experiments in the deep Kolar Gold Fields mines of southern India, from 1960 to 1993. They recorded some of the first atmospheric neutrinos in 1965, then searched for proton decay with iron-and-counter detectors, claiming candidate events that other experiments have not confirmed.
summary.technical: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and Osaka City University underground programme at KGF: cosmic-ray muon depth-intensity measurement to about 2.7 km; 1965 neutrino telescopes at 2300 m; Phase I (140 t, 1600 proportional counters, 7000 hg/cm^2, from end of 1980) and Phase II (260 t, about 4000 counters, 6045 hg/cm^2, from 1985) proton-decay detectors, stopped in 1993 when the mines closed. The collaboration reports a proton lifetime of about 1e31 years; larger detectors set limits near 1e33 years.
